presentingComplaint: High-grade intermittent fever with rigors for 5 days after return from an endemic region
history: 5-day history of paroxysmal high-grade fever preceded by shaking chills and followed by drenching sweats, with headache, myalgia and fatigue. Returned 10 days ago from a rural district in eastern India (Odisha) where he stayed near forested/riverine terrain; did not take chemoprophylaxis and used no bed nets. No dysuria, cough, diarrhoea or rash. No prior similar episodes. No significant PMH, not immunocompromised.
examination: Ill-appearing, febrile and sweating during a paroxysm. Mild pallor and mild scleral icterus. Palpable spleen 2 cm below costal margin. No neck stiffness, no focal neurology (GCS 15), no rash or eschar, chest clear, abdomen soft with no RUQ tenderness or Murphy sign, no peripheral stigmata of endocarditis.
imaging: Not routinely indicated; abdominal ultrasound (if done) shows mild splenomegaly with no focal liver lesion or biliary dilatation
microbiology: Peripheral blood smear (thick + thin): asexual ring forms of Plasmodium falciparum with occasional banana-shaped gametocytes; rapid diagnostic test (HRP-2) positive for P. falciparum. Blood cultures sterile.
citations: WHO Guidelines for the Treatment of Malaria 2015
NVBDCP India National Drug Policy on Malaria 2013
stewardship: Antiparasitic (antimalarial), not antibacterial: uncomplicated P. falciparum should receive artemisinin-based combination therapy - artemether-lumefantrine (or, per Indian NVBDCP policy, artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) plus a single dose of primaquine 0.25 mg/kg as a gametocytocidal agent (after excluding G6PD-relevant risk). No antibacterial agent is indicated.
contraindications: Primaquine contraindicated/needs G6PD testing in G6PD deficiency (haemolysis risk) and in pregnancy
Avoid artemether-lumefantrine with QT-prolonging drugs; caution in significant cardiac conduction disease
Reassess for severe-malaria features - any organ dysfunction mandates IV artesunate rather than oral ACT
edgeCases: Falciparum can progress rapidly to severe/cerebral malaria (coma, seizures), AKI, ARDS or shock - parasitemia >2%, jaundice or altered sensorium should trigger IV artesunate and admission
Smear may be negative during sequestration; repeat smears 12-hourly ×3 and/or RDT if suspicion is high
Mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax infection can be masked; a positive falciparum RDT does not exclude co-infecting vivax needing radical cure
expectedMaiK: Classic paroxysmal fever with rigors, splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia and mild haemolytic jaundice after travel to an endemic area is falciparum malaria until proven otherwise; confirm with blood smear plus RDT and quantify parasitemia, and actively screen for severe-malaria features because falciparum can decompensate quickly.
expectedNextQuestions: Any altered consciousness, seizures, reduced urine output or breathlessness suggesting severe malaria?
Exact travel itinerary, dates, chemoprophylaxis and prior malaria episodes?
expectedInvestigations: Peripheral blood smear (thick and thin) with parasite count/species
regressionAssertions: must flag screening for severe-malaria features before oral therapy
